name: United Arab Emirates
summary_text: The United Arab Emirates screens gender identity against travel documents at entry. In 2025 two Israeli trans women were held for hours at Dubai airport, subjected to X-ray examination to compare their genitals with the female sex recorded in their passports, mocked by staff, denied entry and had their passports confiscated.  Refusals span at least a decade. In March 2022 Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon, runner-up in the 2014 Miss Tiffany Universe contest, was stopped at Dubai immigration, interrogated for nine hours and deported to Thailand before an Expo 2020 appearance because her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman. In August 2016 trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was detained for five hours at Dubai International Airport with her passport confiscated after authorities declined to recognise her gender as legitimate.  The legal framework explicitly acknowledges and penalises nonconformity with traditional gender roles. Transgender expression and unconventional appearance frequently lead to arrest, confinement or expulsion.  Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under Article 409(1)(b) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law, Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021, with a minimum of six months imprisonment and no maximum prescribed. The same provision also criminalises extra-marital heterosexual intercourse.  Cross-dressing liability now centres on access to sex-segregated space. Under Article 412(2) men who disguise themselves as women to enter a women-only space face up to one year imprisonment and a fine of up to AED 10,000. This replaced a broader prior ban on wearing clothing deemed inappropriate for one's sex in any circumstances.  There is no legal gender recognition. No protection exists under any United Arab Emirates law or policy against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. Same-sex marriage is not recognised.  Trans-specific enforcement is documented. In December 2013 two Brazilian transgender women who called Dubai police about prejudice witnessed in a nightclub were themselves arrested for imitating women, held until March 2014, fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported. On 9 August 2017 two Singaporean nationals were convicted in Abu Dhabi and sentenced to one year in prison for attempting to resemble women, then deported on 28 August after nearly three weeks in custody including time in a cell described as designated for effeminate people.  A Brazilian trans woman detained since September 2022 after refusing a police-requested toxicology test remained in prolonged custody in the United Arab Emirates and accused the consulate of negligence in April 2023.  Detention carries documented risk of mistreatment connected to suspected or established same-sex conduct or gender nonconformity, including beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture. Detainees have been held in cells designated for effeminate people. Involuntary medical and psychological measures, including administration of hormonal therapies and detention for forced psychological treatment, have occurred.  Broader enforcement illustrates how public decency provisions are used. Cases include six-month sentences plus deportation for two Indian men in 2012 for consensual sex in a public bus-station toilet, three-year sentences plus deportation for a British man and another man in 2012 for drunken public sex, a one-year sentence plus deportation for a Belgian man in June 2012 after admitting a homosexual relationship with a Filipino man, a police raid breaking up a gathering of 30 men in Dubai on 21 March 2012, and a 2005 Abu Dhabi raid on 26 young men accused of cross-dressing and preparing a gay wedding that resulted in twelve convictions with eleven five-year sentences and one one-year sentence and initial reports that some men were ordered to accept hormone treatments in exchange for lighter sentences.  Seeking police help has exposed complainants to criminal suspicion. In July 2007 in Dubai a 16-year-old French-Swiss boy who was kidnapped and raped was initially treated by police as a suspect. Fear of charge under Article 177 drove him and his family to leave the country. No formal charges were brought against him and he later received AED 15 million in civil compensation. A 17-year-old acquaintance was implicated in luring him, and the family accused the authorities of failing to notify them that one of the rapists was HIV-positive, delaying medical attention. In October 2017 a Scottish tourist arrested for public indecency after touching a man's hip had charges dropped only after intervention by Dubai ruler Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum.  Officials have publicly declared there is no room for homosexual and queer acts in the United Arab Emirates.

name: Argentina
summary_text: Argentina's Gender Identity Law 26,743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after approval in the Chamber of Deputies and in the Senate on 9 May 2012, allows adults to change legal gender, image and birth name on civil registries without surgery, hormone therapy, a psychiatric diagnosis of abnormality, or approval by a doctor or judge. The United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.  On 20 July 2021, Decree 476/2021 required the national civil registry to offer a third gender marker X on all national identity cards and passports, including for non-citizen permanent residents holding Argentine identity cards. Mendoza Province and Santa Fe Province had earlier allowed applicants to leave the sex entry blank.  The same 2012 law grants adults access to sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy through public and private health care plans, with equal access stated for non-binary, transgender and gender non-conforming persons.  In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for persons under age 18. Legal experts described the measure as illegal and unconstitutional and as a setback for adolescents' rights. In April 2025 a Federal Court ruled the ban unconstitutional, restoring access nationwide.  A second February 2025 decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. The sources do not provide its operative terms.  Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since 1887 under Law No. 1,920. Same-sex marriage was legalized on 15 July 2010 with the same benefits and protections as opposite-sex marriage, including adoption since July 2010. A nationwide registered partnership, the union convivencial under the Civil and Commercial Code, has been available since 1 August 2015.  Penal Code Article 80(4), as amended in 2012, imposes life imprisonment for homicide motivated by hatred based on gender identity or expression and on sexual orientation. As of 2019 no national law expressly addressed discrimination or harassment based on gender identity. Outright International records that anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. The national anti-discrimination agency was abolished and shut down in February 2024 as a public-spending measure.  The Observatorio Nacional de Crimenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a record year averaging one every 38 hours. The monitoring group described the figure as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.  In interviews in Buenos Aires on 4 April 2025, reported on 10 April 2025, trans activists including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayan and for Lohana Berkins said the policies of the Milei administration had made the community more vulnerable to violence. Sacayan, a trans activist, was killed in 2015.  On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of Diana Sacayan. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that a cassation court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is currently not applied in the case.  Outright International's Argentina overview, updated 12 March 2026, notes that Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalize marriage equality and that its 2012 law allowed legal gender change without medical procedures or judicial approval. Its current assessment records negative evaluations on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, indicating deterioration.
